— that was at the time when the Confederates (Al-Ahzab)
were making an evil alliance against the Messenger of Allah

and against the Muslims. The Messenger of Allah
feared that the hypocrites, the idolaters, and the Jews would make a
propaganda out of it and try to influence some Muslims of weak hearts.
That was why he urged Zaid not to divorce her, in order not to get
involved into that trial.
Undoubtedly this hesitation and
partiality were alien to the character of the Prophet .
They did not apply to the power of determination and will with which
he had been sent. Allah, the Exalted, blamed him for that by
saying:

"And (remember) when you said
to him (Zaid bin Haritha may
Allah be pleased with him - —
the freed slave of the Prophet )
on whom Allah has bestowed grace (by guiding him to Islam) and
you (O Muhammad
too) have done favour (by
manumitting him), ‘Keep your wife to yourself, and fear Allah.’
But you did hide in yourself (i.e. what Allah has already made
known to you that He will give her to you in marriage) that which Allah
will make manifest, you did fear the people (i.e. Muhammad
married the divorced wife of his
manumitted slave) whereas Allah had a better right that you
should fear him." [33:37]
Finally Zaid divorced Zainab and the
Messenger of Allah
married her at the time he laid siege to Bani Quraiza. That was after
she had finished her Iddat (i.e. period during which a widow
or a divorcee may not remarry). Allah Himself had already
ordained it, and so gave him no other alternative. Allah had
even started the marriage Himself by saying:

"So when Zaid had accomplished
his desire from her (i.e. divorced her), We gave her to you in
marriage, so that (in future) there may be no difficulty to the
believers in respect of (the marriage of) the wives of their adopted
sons when the latter have no desire to keep them (i.e. they have
divorced them)." [33:37]
And that was in order to break down
the tradition of child adoption in practice after He had done it in
words:

"Call them (adopted sons) by
(the names of) their fathers, that is more just near Allah."
[33:5]
"Muhammad ()
is not the father of any man among you, but he is the Messenger of Allah,
and the last (end) of the Prophets." [33:40]
Lots of deeply-rooted traditions
cannot be uprooted or demolished or even adjusted by mere words. They
must be matched and associated with the action of the advocate of the
Message himself.
This could be perceived through the
deeds practised by the Muslims at Al-Hudaibiyah ‘Umrah
(Lesser Pilgrimage) during which ‘Urwah bin Mas‘ud
Al-Thaqafi saw certain Muslims tend to pick up any expectoration that
fell down from the Prophet .
He also saw them race to the water of his ablution and they almost
quarrelled for it. There were others who competed to pledge allegiance
to death and some others pledged not to flee from (the battlefield).
Among those people, were eminent Companions like ‘Umar and Abu
Bakr, who although dedicated all their lives to the Prophet
and to the cause of Islam, but refused to carry out the Messenger’s
ordres with respect to slaughtering sacrificial animals after the
ratification of Al-Hudaibiyah Peace Treaty, the thing that perturbed
and caused the Prophet
to feel anxious. However, when Umm Salamah - may Allah be pleased with
her - advised that he take the initiative and sacrifice his animals,
his followers raced to follow his example; a clear evidence in support
of the saying: Actions speak louder than words, in the process of
exterminating a deeply-established tradition.
Hypocrites aroused a lot of
suspicions and made a broad false propaganda against that marriage.
Their acts and talks about that marriage had ill-effects on those
Muslims whose Faith was still weak, particularly that Zainab was the
fifth wife — and the Noble Qur’an limited the number
up to four only; Zaid was traditionally his son, and so a father
marrying his son’s divorcee was a heinous sin in the eyes of the
Arabians.
Al-Ahzab Surah was
revealed to shed full light on the two issues, i.e. Islam does not
recognize adoption of children, and the Prophet
is given (by Allah) more freedom as regards the number of wives
he can hold than other Muslims in order to achieve noble and
honourable purposes.
However, the treatment of the
Messenger of Allah
to his wives was of honourable, noble, and superb nature. His wives
were on tops in respect of honour, satisfaction, patience, modesty,
and service (that is to say the performance of housework and marriage
duties). Although the Messenger’s house-life was hard and
unbearable, none of his wives complained. Anas said about the Prophet’s
life: "According to my knowledge, the Messenger of Allah

has never tasted a thin flattened loaf in all his lifetime, nor has he
ever seen with his own eyes roasted mutton."[]
‘Aishah said: "Over two
months have elapsed — during which we have seen three crescents —
and yet no fire has been kindled in the houses of the Messenger of Allah

(i.e. they did not cook food)." "What did you eat to sustain
yourselves?" ‘Urwah asked. She said "The two blacks:
dates and water"[].
Lots of information about the hard life of the Prophet
were told.
In spite of these hardships, straits
and adversity of life in the house of the Prophet ,
none of his wives uttered a word of complaint worthy of reproach —
but once. This exception was required by human instinctive
inclinations. However, it was not so important and consequently it did
not require the decree of a legislative rule. Allah has given
them an opportunity to choose between two things, as clearly stated in
the following verses:

"O Prophet (Muhammad )!
Say to your wives: ‘If you desire the life of this world, and its
glitter, — then come! I will make a provision for you and set you
free in a handsome manner (divorce). But if you desire Allah and
His Messenger, and the Home of the Hereafter, then verily, Allah
has prepared for Al-Muhsinat (good doers) amongst you an
enormous reward.’" [33:28,29]
They were so noble and honest that
none of them preferred ‘the life of this world and its glitter’
to the abode in the Hereafter.
Although they were many in number,
nothing of the dispute occurrences that normally happen among
co-wives, took place in their houses. Very few cases could be the only
exception; but they were quite normal. Allah reproached them for
that, so they ceased to do such a thing. This incident is mentioned in
At-Tahreem Chapter:

"O Prophet! Why do you ban (for
yourself) that which Allah has made lawful to you …"
[66:1] (to the end of the fifth verse).
Discussing polygamy — in my
opinion — is not a necessity; since a person who is familiar with
the Europeans, and indecent practices, sufferings, wickedness, their
sorrows and distresses, the horrible crimes they commit in this
respect as well as the trials, the disasters that they are involved
in, and which emanate directly from their disregard of the principle
of polygamy form a good reason (to justify the soundness of polygamy).
The distorted picture of life in Europe with the ill-practices
featuring it, could truthfully justify the existence and practice of
polygamy. In this, there are Divine signs for all people possessed of
lucid mind.
The Prophet ,
Attributes and Manners
The Prophet
combined both perfection of creation and perfection of manners.
This impression on people can be
deduced by the bliss that overwhelmed their hearts and filled them
with dignity. Men’s dignity, devotion and estimation of the
Messenger of Allah
were unique and matchless. No other man in the whole world has been so
honoured and beloved. Those who knew him well, were fascinated and
enchanted by him. They were ready to sacrifice their lives for the
sake of saving a nail of his from hurt or injury. Being privileged by
lots of prerogatives of perfection that no one else had been endowed
with, his Companions found that he was peerless and so they loved him.
Here we list a brief summary of the
versions about his beauty and perfection. To encompass all which is,
addmittedly, beyond our power.
Beauty of Creation:
Describing the Messenger of Allah
,
who passed by her tent on his journey of migration, Umm Ma‘bad
Al-Khuza‘iyah said to her husband:

"He was innocently bright and
had broad countenance. His manners were fine. Neither was his belly
bulging out nor was his head deprived of hair. He had black attractive
eyes finely arched by continuous eyebrows. His hair glossy and black,
inclined to curl, he wore long. His voice was extremely commanding.
His head was large, well formed and set on a slender neck. His
expression was pensive and contemplative, serene and sublime. The
stranger was fascinated from the distance, but no sooner he became
intimate with him than this fascination was changed into attachment
and respect. His expression was very sweet and distinct. His speech
was well set and free from the use of superfluous words, as if it were
a rosary of beads. His stature was neither too high nor too small to
look repulsive. He was a twig amongst the two, singularly bright and
fresh. He was always surrounded by his Companions. Whenever he uttered
something, the listeners would hear him with rapt attention and
whenever he issued any command, they vied with each other in carrying
it out. He was a master and a commander. His utterances were marked by
truth and sincerity, free from all kinds of falsehoods and lies."[]

‘Ali bin Abi Talib describing
him said: "The Messenger of Allah
was neither excessively tall nor extremely short. He was medium height
among his friends. His hair was neither curly nor wavy. It was in
between. It was not too curly nor was it plain straight. It was both
curly and wavy combined. His face was not swollen or meaty-compact. It
was fairly round. His mouth was white. He had black and large eyes
with long haired eyelids. His joints (limbs) and shoulder joints were
rather big. He had a rod-like little hair extending from his chest
down to his navel, but the rest of his body was almost hairless. He
had thick hand palms and thick fingers and toes. At walking, he lifted
his feet off the ground as if he had been walking in a muddy remainder
of water. When he turned, he turned all. The Prophethood Seal was
between his shoulders. He is the Seal of Prophets, the most generous
and the bravest of all.
His speech was the most reliable. He
was the keenest and the most attentive to people’s trust and was
very careful to pay people’s due in full. The Prophet
was the most tractable and the
most yielding companion, seeing him unexpectedly you fear him and
venerate him. He who has acquaintance with him will like him. He who
describes him says:

‘I have never seen such a
person neither before nor after seeing him.’ "[]

Jabir bin Samurah reported that Allah’s
Messenger
had a broad face with reddish (wide) eyes and lean heels.[]
Abu At-Tufail said: "He was
white, good-looking. He was neither fat nor thin; neither tall nor
short."
Anas bin Malik said: "He had
unfolded hands and was pink-coloured. He was neither white nor brown.
He was rather whitish. In both his head and beard there were as many
as twenty grey hairs, besides some grey hairs at his temples." In
another version: "and some scattered white hairs in his head."[]
Abu Juhaifa said: "I have seen
some grey colour under his lower lip." Al-Bara’ said: "He
was of medium height, broad-shouldered, his hair went up to his
earlobes. I saw him dressed in a red garment and I (assure you) I have
never seen someone more handsome. At first he used to let his hair
loose so as to be in compliance with the people of the Book; but later
on he used to part it."[]
Al-Bara’ also said: "He had
the most handsome face and the best character." When he was
asked: "Was the Messenger’s face sword-like?" "No,"
he said: "it was moon-like." But in another version: he
said, "His face was round." Ar-Rabi‘ bint Muawwidh
said: "Had you seen him, you would have felt that the sun was
shining." Jabir bin Samurah said, "I saw him at one
full-moony night. I looked at him. He was dressed in a red garment. I
compared him with the moon and found that — for me — he was
better than the moon."[]
Abu Huraira said: "I have never
seen a thing nicer than the Messenger of Allah .
It seems as if the sunlight were moving within his face. I have never
seen one who is faster in pace than the Messenger of Allah
.
It seemed as if the earth had folded itself up to shorten the distance
for him. For we used to wear ourselves out while he was at full ease."[]
Ka‘b bin Malik said: "When
he was pleased, his face would shine with so bright light that you
would believe that it was a moon-piece."[]Once
he sweated hot at ‘Aishah’s, and the features of his face
twinkled; so I recited a poem by Abu Kabeer Al-Hudhali:

"If you watch his
face-features, you will see them twinkling like the lightning of an
approaching rain."[]

Whenever Abu Bakr saw him he would
say:

"He is faithful, chosen (by Allah),
and calls for forgiveness. He shines like a full-moon light when it is
far from dark (clouds)."[]

‘Umar used to recite verses by
Zuhair describing Haram bin Sinan:

"Were you other than a human
being, you would be a lighted moon at a full-moon night."

Then he would add: "Thus was the
Messenger of Allah .[]

When he got angry his face would go
so red that you would think it were "an inflected red skin-spot
with pomegranate grains on both cheeks."[]
Jabir bin Samurah said: "His
legs were gentle, delicate and in conformity. His laughter is no more
than smiling. Looking at him will make you say ‘He is black-eyed
though he is not so.’"[]
Ibn Al-‘Abbas said: "His
two front teeth were splitted so whenever he speaks, light goes
through them. His neck was as pure and silvery as a neck of doll. His
eyelids were long haired but his beard was thick. His forehead was
broad; but his eyebrows were like the metal piece attached to a lance,
but they were unhorned. His nose was high-tipped, middle-cambered with
narrow nostrils. His cheeks were plain, but he had (little hair)
running down like a rod from his throat to his navel. He had hair
neither on his abdomen nor on his chest except some on his arms and
shoulders. His chest was broad and flatted. He had long forearms with
expansive palms of the hand. His legs were plain straight and
stretching down. His other limbs were straight too. The two hollows of
his soles hardly touch the ground. When he walks away he vanishes
soon; but he walks at ease (when he is not in a hurry). The way he
walks seems similar to one who is leaning forwards and is about to
fall down."[]
Anas said: "I have never touched
silk or a silky garment softer than the palm of the Prophet’s
;
nor have I smelt a perfume or any scent nicer than his." In
another version, "I have never smelt ambergris nor musk nor any
other thing sweeter than the scent and the smell of the Messenger of
Allah ."

Abu Juhaifa said: "I took his
hand and put it on my head and I found that it was colder than ice and
better scented than the musk perfume."[]
Jabir bin Samurah — who was a
little child then — said: "When he wiped my cheek, I felt it
was cold and scented as if it had been taken out of a shop of a
perfume workshop."[]
Anas said, "His sweat was
pearl-like." Umm Sulaim said: "His sweat smelt nicer than
the nicest perfume."
Jabir said: "Whoever pursues a
road that has been trodden by the Messenger of Allah ,
will certainly scent his smell and will be quite sure that the
Messenger of Allah has
already passed it." The Seal of Prophethood, which was similar in
size to a pigeon’s egg, was between his shoulders on the left
side having spots on it like moles.[]
The Perfection of Soul and
Nobility:
The Prophet
was noted for superb eloquence and fluency in Arabic. He was
remarkable in position and rank. He was an accurate, unpretending
straightforward speaker. He was well-versed in Arabic and quite
familiar with the dialects and accents of every tribe. He spoke with
his entertainers using their own accents and dialects. He mastered and
was quite eloquent at both bedouin and town speech. So he had the
strength and eloquence of bedouin language as well as the clarity and
the decorated splendid speech of town. Above all, there was the
assistance of Allah embodied in the revealed verses of the Qur’an.
His stamina, endurance and
forgiveness — out of a commanding position — his patience
and standing what he detested — these were all talents,
attributes and qualities Allah Himself had brought him on. Even
wise men have their flaws, but the Messenger of Allah ,
unlike everybody, the more he was hurt or injured, the more clement
and patient he became. The more insolence an ignorant anybody
exercised against him the more enduring he became.
‘Aishah said:
"The Messenger of Allah
,
whenever he is given the opportunity to choose between two affairs, he
always chooses the easiest and the most convenient. But if he is
certain that it is sinful, he will be as far as he could from it. He
has never avenged himself; but when the sanctity of Allah is
violated he would. That would be for Allah’s not for
himself. He is the last one to get angry and the first to be
satisfied. His hospitality and generosity were matchless. His gifts
and endowments manifest a man who does not fear poverty."[]
Ibn‘Abbas said: "The
Prophet
was the most generous. He is usually most generous of all times in
Ramadan, the times at which the angel Gabriel - peace be upon him -
comes to see him. Gabriel used to visit him every night of Ramadan and
review the Qur’an with him. Verily the Messenger of Allah

is more generous at giving bounty or charity than the blowing wind."

Jabir said:
"The Prophet
would never deny anything he was asked for."[]
His courage, his succour and his
might are distinguishable. He was the most courageous. He witnessed
awkward and difficult times and stoodfast at them. More than once
brave men and daring ones fled away leaving him alone; yet he stood
with full composure facing the enemy without turning his back. All
brave men must have experienced fleeing once or have been driven off
the battlefield at a round at a time except the Prophet .
‘Ali said: "Whenever the fight grew fierce and the eyes of
fighters went red, we used to resort to the Prophet
for succour. He was always the closest to the enemy."[]
Anas said: "One night the people
of Madinah felt alarmed. People went out hurriedly towards the source
of sound, but the Prophet
had already gone ahead of them. He was on the horseback of Abu Talhah
which had no saddle over it, and a sword was slung round his neck, and
said to them: ‘There was nothing to be afraid for.’"[]
He was the most modest and the first
one to cast his eyes down. Abu Sa‘id Al-Khudri said: "He
was shier than a virgin in her boudoir. When he hates a thing we read
it on his face.[]
He does not stare at anybody’s face. He always casts his eyes
down. He looks at the ground more than he looks sky-wards. His utmost
looks at people are glances. He is willingly and modestly obeyed by
everybody. He would never name a person whom he had heard ill-news
about — which he hated. Instead he would say: ‘Why do
certain people do so....’"
Al-Farazdaq verse of poem fits him
very much and the best one to be said of:

"He casts his eyes modestly but
the eyes of others are cast down due to his solemnity, and words issue
out of his mouth only while he is smiling."
The Prophet
is the most just, the most decent, the most truthful at speech, and
the honestest of all. Those who have exchanged speech with him, and
even his enemies, acknowledge his noble qualities. Even before the
Prophethood he was nicknamed Al-Ameen (i.e. the truthful, the
truthworthy). Even then — in Al-Jahiliyah — they
used to turn to him for judgement and consultation. In a version by
At-Tirmidhi, he says that ‘Ali had said that he had been told by
Abu Jahl that he (Abu Jahl) said to the Messenger of Allah
:
"We do not call you a liar; but we do not have faith in what you
have brought."[]In
His Book, Allah, the Exalted, said about them:

"It is not you that they deny,
but it is the Verses (the Qur’an) of Allah that the
Zalimun (polytheists and wrong-doers) deny." [6:33]

Even when Heraclius asked Abu Sufyan:
"Have you ever accused him of lying before the ministry of
Prophethood?" Abu Sufyan said: "No."
He was most modest and far from being
arrogant or proud. He forbade people to stand up at his presence as
other people usually do for their kings.
Visiting the poor, the needy and
entertaining them are some of his habits. If a slave invited him, he
would accept the invitation. He always sat among his friends as if he
were an ordinary person of them. ‘Aishah said that he used to
repair his shoes, sew or mend his dress and to do what ordinary men
did in their houses. After all, he was a human being like others. He
used to check his dress (lest it has some insects on). Milking the
she-sheep and catering for himself were some of his normal jobs.[]
The Prophet
was the most truthful to his pledges, and it is one of his qualities
to establish good and steady relationship with his relatives — ‘Silat-Ar-Rahim’.
He is the most merciful, gentle and amiable to all people. His way of
living is the simplest one. Ill-manners and indecency are two
qualities completely alien to him. He was decent, and did not call
anybody names. He was not the sort of person who cursed or made noise
in the streets. He did not exchange offences with others. He pushed
back an offence or an error by forgiveness and overlooking. Nobody was
allowed to walk behind him (i.e. as a bodyguard). He did not feel
himself superior to others not even to his slaves (men or women) as
far as food or clothes were concerned.
Whoever served him should be served
by him too. ‘Ugh’ (an utterance of complaint) is a word that
had never been said by him to his servant; nor was his servant blamed
for doing a thing or leaving it undone. Loving the poor and the needy
and entertaining them or participating in their funerals were things
the Prophet always
observed. He never contempted or disgraced a poor man for his poverty.
Once he was travelling with his Companions and when it was time to
have food prepared, he asked them to slaughter a she-sheep. A man
said: I will slaughter it, another one said: I will skin it out. A
third said: I will cook it. So the Messenger of Allah
said: I will collect wood for
fire. They said: "No. We will suffice you that work." "I
know that you can do it for me, but I hate to be privileged. Allah
hates to see a slave of his privileged to others." So he went and
collected fire-wood.[]
Let us have some of the description
of Hind bin Abi Halah: "The Messenger of Allah
was continually sad, thinking perpetually. He had no rest (i.e. for
long). He only spoke when it was necessary. He would remain silent for
a long time and whenever he spoke, he would end his talk with his
jawbone but not out of the corners of his mouth, i.e. (snobbishly).
His speech was inclusive. He spoke inclusively and decisively. It was
not excessive nor was it short of meaning. It was amiable. It was in
no way hard discoroning. He glorified the bounty of Allah; even
if it were little. If he had no liking for someone’s food, he
would neither praise nor criticize.
He was always in full control of his
temper and he would never get seemed angry unless it was necessary. He
never got angry for himself nor did he avenge himself. It was for Allah’s
sanctity and religion that he always seemed angry.
When he pointed at a thing he would
do so with his full hand-palm, and he would turn it round to show
surprise. If he were angry he would turn both his body and face aside.
When he was pleased, he cast his eyes down. His laughter was mostly
smiling. It was then that his teeth which were like hail-stones were
revealed.
He never spoke unless it was
something closely relevant to him. He confirmed the brotherhood
relationship among his Companions; and thus he made them intimate and
did not separate them or implant enmity among them. Those who were
honourable with their peoples, were honoured and respected by him and
were assigned rulers over their own peoples. His cheerfulness was
never withdrawn at anyone’s face; even at those whom he warned
his people from or those whom he himself was on the alert of. He
visited friends and inquired about people’s affairs. He confirmed
what was right and criticized the awful and tried to undermine it. He
was moderate in all affairs. He was equal to others and was not
privileged. He would never act heedlessly, lest the others should get
heedless. Each situation was dealt with in its proper due.
Righteousness was his target; so he
was never short of it nor indifferent to it. People who sat next to
him were the best of their people and the best of them all were —
for him — those who provided common consultations. For him, the
greatest ones and the highest in ranks were the best at providing
comfort and co-ordination and succour. Remembrance (of Allah)
was a thing he aimed at and established whenever he sat down or stands
up. No certain position was assigned for him to sit on. He sits at the
end of the group, seated next to the last sitter in the place. He
ordered people to do the same. He entertained his participiants in
social gatherings alike so that the one addressed would think that
there was no one honoured by the Prophet
but himself. He whoever sat next
to him or interrupted him in order to ask for his advice about an
affair of his, would be the first to start the talk and the one to end
it. The Prophet
would listen to him patiently till he ended his speech. He never
denied a request to anyone, if unapproachable, then few gratifying
words would work, instead.
His magnanimity, broad mindedness his
tolerance could embrace all people and entitled him to be regarded as
father for them all. In justice, all of them were almost equal. Nobody
was better than another except on the criterion of Allah
fearing. A favoured one, to him, was the most Allah fearing. His
assembly was a meeting of clemency, timidness, patience and honesty.
Voices were not raised in rows or riots. Inviolable things were never
violable. Fearing Allah and worship were their means to sympathy
and compassion. They used to esteem the old and have mercy on the
young. They assisted the needy and entertained strangers.
The Messenger of Allah
was always cheerful, easy, pleasant-tempered and lenient. He was never
rude or rough nor clamorous or indecent. He was neither a reproacher
nor a praiser. He overlooked what he did not desire, yet you would
never despair of him. Three qualities he disposed of: hypocrisy,
excessiveness, and what was none of his concern. People did not fear
him in three areas: — for they were not qualities or habits of
his —: He never disparaged, or reproached nor did he seek the
defects or shortages of others. He only spoke things whose reward was
Divinely desirable. When he spoke, his listeners would attentively
listen casting down their heads. They only spoke when he was silent.
They did not have disputes or arguments about who was to talk. He who
talked in his presence would be listened to by everybody till he
finished his talk. Their talk would be about the topic discussed or
delivered by their first speaker. The Messenger of Allah
used to laugh at what they laughed at and admired what they used to
admire. He would always show patience with a stranger’s harshness
at talk. He used to say:

"When you see a person seeking
an object earnestly, assist him to get his need. And never ask for a
reward except from the reward-Giver, i.e. Allah."[]

Kharijah bin Zaid said: "The
Prophet
was the most honoured among the people with whom he sat. His limbs
could hardly be seen. He was often silent and rarely talked when
speech was not a necessity. He turned away from those whose speech was
rude or impolite. His laughter was no more than a smile. His speech,
which was decisive, it was neither excessive nor incomplete. Out of
reverence and esteem and following the example of their Prophet
,
the Companions’ laughter at his presence — was smiling, as
well."[]
On the whole the Prophet
was ornamented with peerless attributes of perfection. No wonder to be
like that for he was brought up, educated and taught (the Qur’an)
by Allah. He was even praised by Allah:

"And verily, you (O Muhammad

) are on an exalted standard of character." [68:4]

Those were the attributes and
qualities that the Prophet

enjoyed which made the hearts of souls of the people close to him,
draw near to him and love him. Those traits made him so popular that
the restraint and enmity of his people grew less and they started to
embrace Islam in large crowds.
This description is in fact no more
than a rapid review or rather short brief lines of Muhammad’s
aspects of full perfection. Trying to encompass the whole perfect
picture of the Prophet .
No one can ever claim to be possessed of full knowledge or complete
mastery of the great attributes of the greatest man in this universe.
No one can ever give this man, the top of perfection, his due
descrpition. He was a man who always sought Allah’s light,
to such an extent that he was wholly imbued with the Qur’anic
approach.

O Allah! send your blessings
(and the Holy Words of Yours) upon Muhammad and the family of
Muhammad, as You have send blessings upon Ibrahim and the family
of Ibrahim. You are worthy of all praise, All Glorious.

O Allah! bless Muhammad and the
family of Muhammad as You have already blessed Ibrahim and the
family of Ibrahim. You are worthy of all praise, All Glorious.

chapters.title: The Pledges of Aqabah
chapters.content:
Before the flight to Madinah there were two quiet meetings on a dark hillside, and between them a single unarmed teacher. Without those meetings there would have been no Hijrah, no Madinan state, and the ten years of struggle that followed would never have taken their historical shape. The Pledges of Aqabah — the first with twelve men, the second with seventy-three men and two women — are the hinge on which the whole Sirah turns.

The men of Yathrib had known civil war. For generations the Arab tribes of the oasis — Aws and Khazraj — and their Jewish neighbours had bled one another in a succession of bitter feuds, and the battle of Bu'ath, fought only a few years earlier, had left every household mourning. At the pilgrimage season the Prophet (ﷺ) went where all Arabs went, to the fair at Aqabah near Mina, and presented himself to the pilgrim delegations, saying: "Which tribe will shelter me, that I may convey the word of my Lord?" Most passed him by.

Then came six men of Khazraj. The season of pilgrimage had brought them to Makkah, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) spoke with them about Islam and recited the Qur'an. They looked at one another and whispered: "Know, by Allah, that this may well be the very thing that will end the war between us and the Jews." Allah had prepared their hearts through weariness of blood. They accepted Islam that night and returned to Yathrib carrying the light with them, and the news of faith began to travel between the two cities with every pilgrim caravan.

The next year the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent with them Mus'ab bin 'Umair (may Allah be pleased with him) — the young Makkan aristocrat who had known silk garments all his life and now owned only his faith — to teach the Qur'an and instruct the people. He was the first ambassador of Islam, and he carried no sword and demanded nothing. Lodging first with As'ad bin Zurarah, he recited and taught and answered objections with the Book of Allah alone.

His most famous test came at the hands of Usaid bin Hudair, an Aws chieftain who came to drive the "corrupter" out of his people's quarter. Mus'ab answered gently: "Will you sit and listen? If you like what you hear, accept it; and if you dislike it, I will leave." Usaid speared his spear into the ground and sat. When he rose, his face had changed. Sa'd bin Mu'adh, watching from a distance, was enraged at what the stranger had done to his friend, and came storming — and sat, and listened, and rose with his face changed also. That evening both chieftains had accepted Islam, and by nightfall not a house in the quarter of Banu Abdul-Ashhal remained but that Islam was mentioned in it. Sa'd bin Mu'adh would one day die a martyr of Uhud, and the tradition relates that the throne of the Merciful shook at his funeral; but on that day in Yathrib he was simply one more man whose heart the Qur'an had opened.

At the pilgrimage season of the twelfth year of the Prophethood — the summer of 621 CE — twelve men of Yathrib came down to Aqabah and gave the first Pledge of Aqabah, known as the Pledge of Women because it contained no duty of fighting. They pledged that they would associate nothing with Allah, not steal, not commit adultery, not kill their children, not bring a slander they had forged themselves, and not disobey the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in what was right. "Whoever fulfils this," the Prophet (ﷺ) told them, "his reward is with Allah; and whoever falls short in any of it and Allah conceals it, his affair is with Allah — if He wills He will punish him, and if He wills He will forgive him."

Then he chose from among the twelve twelve leaders — naqib — to carry the affairs of their people, with As'ad bin Zurarah at their head, and he said: "You are sureties over your people, as the disciples of 'Isa bin Maryam were sureties over their people, and I am a surety over my people." Mus'ab remained in Yathrib, and Islam entered every quarter of the city, so that there was no household of the Aws or the Khazraj in which the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was not spoken of.

The second Pledge of Aqabah came at the following pilgrimage season, the thirteenth year of the Prophethood — June 622 CE. It was larger, bolder and heavier in consequence. Seventy-three men and two women of Yathrib — among them Nusaybah bint Ka'b, known as Umm 'Umarah, who would later defend the Prophet (ﷺ) with her own body at Uhud, and Asma bint 'Amr, Umm Mani' — slipped away by night from their camps and made their way to the appointed place at Aqabah, taking care not to wake their fellow pilgrims.

They had barely settled when a last challenge came. Al-'Abbas bin 'Abdul-Muttalib, the Prophet's uncle, who still held to the religion of his fathers, had come to stand beside his nephew and safeguard his interests. "Muhammad," he said, "is exalted in his own family. If you are resolved to carry him off and defend him against his opponents, you are responsible for it; but if you cannot carry out what you pledge, then leave him now, for he is safe where he is." Their spokesman al-Bara' bin Ma'rur answered: "We have heard your words, and by Him who sent you with the truth we have before us today what no people have before them: swords are drawn and drawn anew, and men have met in the open. If you will test us with these things, we will test you with them, until Allah makes you victorious; for we are men of war and men of lineage, men of the chase." The Prophet (ﷺ) smiled and said: "Pledge to me that you will protect me from all sides, as you protect your women and children." Al-Bara' took his hand and pledged.

Ka'b bin Malik, the poet, who lived to old age and outlived the Prophet (ﷺ), remembered the night all his life: "We took the pledge while we hid ourselves among the rocks, seventy-three men, and I was the youngest of them and the thirteenth in the row." The pledge of this night was the pledge of war and of defence — to hear and to obey in ease and hardship, to spend in plenty and poverty, to enjoin right and forbid wrong, and to stand for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) against the whole of mankind if they should set upon him, so long as they were not separated from him by rivers and mountain passes. In return the Prophet (ﷺ) gave them his covenant: "Paradise." And he chose twelve naqib once more, over their tribes and clans, to lead them — men such as 'Ubadah bin as-Samit, Sa'd bin 'Ubadah, al-Mundhir bin 'Amr and Usayd bin Hudair.

As the men of Yathrib returned to their camps before dawn, the Quraysh finally understood what had been happening for two seasons. They pursued the last stragglers and seized Sa'd bin 'Ubadah, and they had already learned from the companions of 'Abdullah bin Ubayy — the future chief of the hypocrites — that their city had given its heart to the Prophet of Makkah. The secret could not be kept any longer, and it did not need to be. Within weeks the persecution in Makkah reached its climax with a plot to kill the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and the stage was set for the Hijrah.

It is worth pausing on what the two pledges actually were. They were not a treaty of conquest, and Madinah did not promise Muhammad (ﷺ) a throne. They were the vows of free men and free women who accepted a Message and then accepted the cost of it. The first pledge bound them to moral law; the second bound them to solidarity. Between them stood Mus'ab bin 'Umair with a Book and a gentle tongue, proving that hearts are won by teaching, not by force. When the migration came, the men and women of Aqabah turned their city into the first abode of Islam in history — and Yathrib was no more; it became Madinat an-Nabi, the City of the Prophet (ﷺ).

Lessons and Reflections

• Great transformations begin with a few individuals. The future of all Islam rested that night on twelve men, and then on seventy-three — people of no state, no army and no treasury, only of a promise.

• The first pledge shows that faith begins with morals: no idolatry, no theft, no adultery, no infanticide, no slander. Community strength is built on personal integrity.

• Mus'ab bin 'Umair demonstrates the power of character and education in da'wah: he won the chieftains of Yathrib without a single argument of force, answering every attack with patience and the Qur'an.

• Women were present and pledged at Aqabah. Nusaybah bint Ka'b took the same covenant as the men, and later stood in the battlefield of Uhud — participation of believing women in the community's affairs is woven into Islam from its very first institutions.

• Al-'Abbas's caution and the Ansar's answer teach honesty in commitment: they were warned plainly of the cost, and they accepted it with open eyes. A pledge given knowingly is a pledge that endures.

chapters.title: The Hijrah: Flight to Madinah
chapters.content:
Every age of Islam counts its years from one event, and that event is not a battle or a coronation but a journey — a man and his closest friend slipping out of a besieged city at night, walking south away from their destination, hiding three days in a cave, and then crossing the desert to a city of strangers. The Hijrah of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) from Makkah to Madinah in the year 622 CE was the moment the persecuted Message acquired a home, and 'Umar bin al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) later fixed the Muslim calendar to begin from it, because it was then that the faith of individuals became the faith of a community.

The council of the Quraysh at Dar an-Nadwah had resolved the matter with cold logic. Banu Hashim could avenge a murder on a single clan, so the clans would strike together: one strong young man from every tribe, each armed with a sharp sword, would surround the Prophet's house and strike as one man, so that his blood would be divided among all the tribes and Bani Hashim could not take revenge on them all. The plan was agreed — but Allah had already exposed it. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) received the permission of his Lord to migrate, went at noon to the house of his friend Abu Bakr as-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him) — who had kept two she-camels fed and ready for four months, waiting for this very day — and said: "I have been given permission to depart." "O Messenger of Allah," Abu Bakr asked, "in company?" "In company," he answered.

Gabriel came to the Prophet (ﷺ) with the plot of the Quraysh, and told him not to sleep that night in his bed. 'Ali bin Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him) wrapped himself in the Prophet's green mantle and lay down where he was accustomed to sleep, while the young men of the clans waited outside for the man they believed lay within. When the Prophet (ﷺ) left the house he recited the opening verses of Surah Ya-Sin and, casting dust on the heads of the ambush, went out in their full sight — and Allah removed them from seeing him. He lifted the dust from his bed and returned to it, and in the morning the Quraysh, discovering 'Ali in the bed, realised their prey had gone.

The Prophet (ﷺ) and Abu Bakr did not travel toward Madinah. They went south, to the mountain of Thawr, climbing it by a path no guide knew, and hid in its cave for three nights while the manhunt raged. Abu Bakr had engaged 'Abdullah bin Uraiqit, an experienced guide of the tribe of Ad-Dayl who was not yet a Muslim, with full trust: the guide brought the two she-camels after three nights, and led them by the rarely-used coastal road. Every evening Asma bint Abi Bakr (may Allah be pleased with her) carried food to the cave — when her sash gave way she tore it in two, and from that day she was called Dhat an-Nitaqayn, the woman of the two belts. Amir bin Fuhairah, Abu Bakr's freed slave, grazed his flocks past the mountain at evening and morning, letting the sheep efface the footprints and carrying milk.

The most dramatic moment of those three nights came when a Quraysh search party, led by men who knew the mountain, stood at the very mouth of the cave. Through the opening they could be seen and heard. Abu Bakr whispered his fear — not for himself, but for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "If one of them looks down at his feet he will see us." The Prophet (ﷺ) answered with the words Allah soon sealed in revelation: "What do you think of two, the third of whom is Allah?" Then came the verse of Surah At-Tawbah: "If you do not aid him — Allah has already aided him, when the disbelievers drove him out, the second of two, when they two were in the cave, when he said to his companion: Do not grieve; indeed Allah is with us." [9:40] The searchers went away, and trust had triumphed where numbers could not.

For a hundred camels the Quraysh had promised for each of the two, and the prize-drawn hunters went out in every direction. Among them was Suraqah bin Malik, who sent his companions back on a false alarm so that the reward might be his alone, and rode after the travellers on his swift mare. As he drew near, his horse stumbled and sank to its chest in the sand, throwing him down. Three times he tried, three times the sand received the animal, and a pillar of dust rose to the sky. Suraqah understood: this matter was of another order than raiding. He called out for a covenant of safety, promising to mislead his own people, and asked the Prophet (ﷺ) for a letter of security. The Prophet (ﷺ) granted it — and gave him a prophecy that sounded impossible: "How will you feel, Suraqah, when you wear the bracelets of Kisra, the emperor of Persia?" Years later, after the fall of the Persian empire, the spoils of Kisra were brought to 'Umar, and Suraqah was summoned to wear the very bracelets of the great Khosrow. The desert tale had become public history.

The journey went on: past Usfan and Qudaid, where 'Az-Zubair's caravan met them with white garments and greeted them with the news of gladness; the tent of Umm Ma'bad al-Khuza'iyah, whose goat the Prophet (ﷺ) milked when it had given nothing, filling a vessel to the brim — she later described the man who had passed her tent in one of the most famous portraits in Arabic literature; and Buraydah bin al-Husayb, who overtook them intending ransom, heard the Message, and accepted Islam with his whole company, walking before the Prophet (ﷺ) as an escort into the city.

On Monday, the eighth of Rabi' al-Awwal in the first year of the Hijrah, the Prophet (ﷺ) reached Quba, on the outskirts of Yathrib, where the people streamed out to greet him, climbing rooftops and calling to one another. There he stayed several days among Banu 'Amr bin 'Awf, and founded the first mosque of Islam — the mosque "founded on taqwa from the first day," which Allah's own words in Surah At-Tawbah honour to this day. 'Ali, who had stayed behind to return the trusts the Makkans had deposited with the Prophet (ﷺ) — for even his enemies had trusted him with their valuables — caught up on foot, his feet swollen and bleeding, and the Prophet (ﷺ) treated his companion's wounds with his own hands.

On Friday the travellers rode out for Yathrib. At the valley of Ranuna', among Banu Salim bin 'Awf, about a hundred worshippers gathered for the first Friday prayer of Islam, and the Prophet (ﷺ) led them in it. Then the whole oasis came out to welcome him — women and children on the rooftops, men on the roads, singing the verses of welcome the tradition has preserved: "Tala'a al-badru 'alayna — the full moon has risen over us." Everyone pressed to take his halter, but he let his she-camel go free, saying: "Leave her, for she is commanded." The camel knelt at last before the door of Abu Ayyub al-Ansari (may Allah be pleased with him), who carried the saddle into his house and became the Prophet's host for the months during which the Prophet's mosque and adjoining rooms were being built upon the plot he bought from two orphan boys of Banu Najjar.

Yathrib was renamed: Madinat an-Nabi, the City of the Prophet (ﷺ). The first acts of the new city were the mosque — the seat of worship, teaching and counsel — the pact of brotherhood, by which every Muhajir was paired with an Ansari brother who shared his home and wealth, and the covenant of Madinah, the written constitution that bound the Muslims, the Jews and the pagan tribes of the oasis into one community with mutual obligations and freedom of religion. A state had been born out of a flight, and the persecuted preacher of Makkah became the head of a society that within one generation would carry his Message from the Atlantic to the Indus.

Lessons and Reflections

• The Hijrah teaches perfect balance between trust in Allah and sound planning: the Prophet (ﷺ) relied completely on his Lord, yet chose an expert guide, stocked food, sent a scout and took every worldly precaution.

• 'Ali's willingness to sleep in the bed, Abu Bakr's four months of preparation, Asma's two belts and Amir's sheep: greatness in Islam's story is often made of small, quiet acts of loyalty.

• 'Abdullah bin Uraiqit was a non-Muslim, hired and trusted with the lives of the two most beloved to Allah — ability and trustworthiness, not creed alone, govern professional dealings in Islam.

• The cave of Thawr is the eternal answer to fear: 'Do not grieve; indeed Allah is with us.' Numbers, arms and walls are not what protect the truth.

• The calendar of the Ummah begins not with a victory but with sacrifice and brotherhood. To be Muslim is, in spirit, to be always making hijrah — migrating away from what Allah forbids toward what He loves.

chapters.title: The Battle of Khaybar
chapters.content:
An hour's march north-east of Madinah, in a volcanic country of black rock and red dates, stood Khaybar — the strongest fortress-city of Arabia, a chain of fortified citadels rising above one of the richest oases of the Hijaz. It was from Khaybar that the exiled Jews of Banu Nadir, above all Huyayy bin Akhtab and Kinana bin ar-Rabi', had financed the Confederates' war on Madinah, stirred the Ghatafan, and kept the north in flames. The Treaty of Hudaybiyyah had just given the Prophet (ﷺ) what he had never had in ten years of war: peace on his southern flank and a free hand in the north. In Muharram of the seventh year after the Hijrah — May or June of 628 CE — he turned that free hand toward the fortress-city, announcing to the Muslims: "This morning, Allah has made me victorious at Khaybar."

The campaign began in secrecy. The Prophet (ﷺ) marched with some fourteen hundred men, the largest body of riders yet to leave Madinah together, and moved by night along roads that avoided the watchmen. When dawn broke the Muslims found themselves at the very edge of the enemy's fields, and the workers coming out with their baskets cried out in terror at the sight. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Allah is greater! Khaybar is destroyed. When we descend upon a people's courtyard, evil is the morning of those who were warned." Then he raised his famous supplication of the morning of Khaybar: "O Allah, Lord of the heavens and of all that they overshadow, Lord of the earths and of all they carry, Lord of the devils and of all they lead astray — I ask You for the good of this town and the good of its people, and I seek refuge in You from its evil and the evil of its people."

Khaybar was not one city but a chain of strongholds — Na'im, As-Sa'b, the castle of Az-Zubair, 'Abi Castle and An-Nizar in the quarter of Ash-Shiqq; then Al-Qamus, Al-Watih and As-Sulalim. The Prophet (ﷺ) reduced them one after another. At Na'im the Jewish champion Marhab — a man of terrible strength, in an Armenian coat of mail, who had learned warfare in Persia and proclaimed himself as Khaybar had never before been tested — came out seeking single combat. 'Amr bin al-Akwa' answered him and fell in the exchange, dying with the sweetness of the words he had spoken that morning as he ate from the army's short rations: "I have found the sweetness of fighting under the shade of spears." Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) declared: "Tomorrow I shall give the banner to a man who loves Allah and His Messenger, and Allah will grant victory at his hands."

That man was 'Ali bin Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him) — who had been detained by an inflammation of his eyes, and whose eyes the Prophet (ﷺ) healed with his own blessed treatment. 'Ali came out against Marhab, and the two champions met in the space between the hosts; and Allah gave 'Ali the victory, and Marhab fell. His brother Yasir took up the challenge and was slain by Az-Zubair bin al-'Awwam. Real fighting then broke out along the fortress line, and one stronghold after another was taken.

The great castle of Al-Qamus, the seat of Kinana bin ar-Rabi', resisted longest. The Prophet (ﷺ) laid siege to it for some fourteen days, and the fortress fell in the end. With it fell Khaybar's resistance. The question of exactly how Al-Qamus was taken — by assault or by stratagem — the scholars of the Sirah relate differently, but the outcome is agreed: Khaybar submitted, its armies broken, its champions dead.

Two scenes from the days after the victory deserve to be remembered. The first is the shepherd boy — a Jewish youth in the service of the fortress, driving his flock, who watched the Muslims and then came to them and declared his faith. The Prophet (ﷺ) asked him where the sheep had grazed; when the boy answered, the army realised every animal had passed among the Muslim soldiers without a single one being taken or even touched during the hunger of the siege. The Prophet (ﷺ) was shown a flock and told it was for the Muslims to eat; he refused to benefit from spoils before the victory was complete — a discipline he enforced on all his men. The second scene concerns Kinana, who had hidden Khaybar's treasury rather than surrender it, and whose concealment was exposed; the wealth of the fortress came into the public treasury. From the captives of Khaybar the Prophet (ﷺ) chose Safiyyah bint Huyayy (may Allah be pleased with her), the daughter of the chief who had led the intrigues against Madinah — he freed her, married her, and made her freedom her bridal gift. She became one of the Mothers of the Believers, and lived to be one of the great narrators of the Prophet's life.

The terms the Prophet (ﷺ) granted Khaybar became the model for all later settlements: the people, now subjects, kept their lands and their religion and agreed to cultivate them in return for half the produce, and the wealth of Fadak, the neighbouring oasis, came similarly under treaty. It was in this season that Surah Al-Hashr descended, prescribing the shares of the public treasury: to Allah and His Messenger, to near kin, to orphans, the needy and the wayfarer, "so that wealth may not merely circulate among the rich among you." [59:7] The fifth of the spoils that belonged to the Prophet (ﷺ) he distributed among the Muslims of Madinah so completely that no household remained without its share.

At the height of the triumph came treachery. A Jewess of Khaybar, Zaynab bint al-Harith, roasted a lamb and envenomed it, asking what part of the animal the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) favoured — and placing the poison where his favour would fall. He took the shoulder, tasted it, and felt its effect; the Companion Bishr bin al-Bara' who had swallowed a morsel died of it. The Prophet (ﷺ) forbade the execution of every Jew of Khaybar for the crime of one, and when Zaynab confessed — saying, "If you were a king I would have spared myself the trouble; but I said, if he is truly a prophet he will be told" — he pardoned her, though the consequences of that poison are said by many physicians of the Sirah to have remained in his body until his death. Even at the table of his greatest victory, mercy kept its hold upon him.

The fall of Khaybar thundered through Arabia. The tribes that had awaited the outcome hastened to make terms, and the anti-Islamic coalition of the north dissolved into treaties. Ja'far bin Abi Talib returned that very season from Abyssinia with the emigrants of the first Hijrah, and the Prophet (ﷺ), who had just given them a share of the spoils, embraced him and wept with joy: "I do not know which of the two makes me happier — their coming or the conquest of Khaybar." Within weeks the Muslims performed the compensatory 'Umrah they had been denied at Hudaybiyyah, entering Makkah for three days with the treaty's permission, and the world could see that the covenant of the previous year had not been weakness but patience.

Lessons and Reflections

• Khaybar shows the difference between enmity and justice: the war was with a hostile alliance, not with a people, and the settlement that followed preserved lives, lands and worship.

• The Prophet's choice of 'Ali — 'a man who loves Allah and His Messenger' — teaches that leadership in Islam is proven by love of Allah before talent, and talent follows love.

• 'Amr bin al-Akwa' is Islam's picture of the believer's heart in hardship: he had called hunger and fighting 'sweeter than honey' the same morning he died of them. Sincerity turns scarcity into sweetness.

• Discipline before victory: not one sheep of the besieged flock was touched by a starving army. Self-restraint in the hour of hunger is the proof of an army of Allah, not merely an army.

• The poisoning of the Prophet (ﷺ) and his pardon of the culprit reveal the limit of vengeance in Islam: guilt is personal, punishment is proportionate, and forgiveness remains open even at the moment of triumph.

chapters.title: The Conquest of Makkah
chapters.content:
For twenty-one years the Quraysh had been the answer to every question about Muhammad (ﷺ). They had mocked him, starved his clan for three years, plotted his murder, hunted him through the desert, and met him in the field at Badr, Uhud and the Trench. In Ramadan of the eighth year after the Hijrah — January 630 CE — the answer changed, and it changed in a way no Arab had imagined an answer could be given: with an army of ten thousand at the gates of their city, and an amnesty no one had asked for.

The immediate cause was a tribal pact. By the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah, Khuza'ah had allied with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and Banu Bakr with the Quraysh. A generation of blood between Banu Bakr and Khuza'ah now flared again, and this time the Quraysh armed their allies in secret — men, weapons and horses supplied by Nawfal bin Mu'awiyah — and Banu Bakr fell upon Khuza'ah at night by the well of al-Wateer, killing more than twenty men. Khuza'ah fled into the sacred precinct, and their pursuers profaned it, crying, "Today is your day! Today we are absolved!" — mocking the very sanctities of the House of Allah they claimed to defend.

'Amr bin Salim al-Khuza'i rode to Madinah with eighty men and stood before the Prophet (ﷺ) reciting verses that ended: "O Allah, we seek the help of the Messenger and the help of the Lord against the insolent reviler." The Quraysh, realising the breach they had made, sent Abu Sufyan himself to Madinah to renew and extend the treaty. He went first to his own daughter Umm Habibah — the Prophet's wife — and when he moved to fold the Prophet's bed she snatched it away: "You are a polytheist and unclean, and this is the bed of the Messenger of Allah." He went to the Prophet (ﷺ) and spoke; no one answered him. He went to Abu Bakr, to 'Umar, to 'Ali, to Fatimah, and found no intercessor. Leaving the mosque he saw the Prophet (ﷺ) performing prayer, and Abu Bakr and 'Umar with him, and said to himself that they had resolved upon war. "Do you not see," 'Ali told him, "the panic in your eyes? There is no security for you." Abu Sufyan returned to Makkah empty-handed — but he had seen enough to know what was coming.

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) made his preparations in the dark. He called upon Madinah to prepare swiftly and secretly, praying: "O Allah, take the eyes and spies of the Quraysh from us until we take their land by surprise." He despatched Abu Qatadah with a detachment toward Batn Idam, a feint that drew the watchers' attention elsewhere. It was during this time that the affair of Hatib bin Abi Balta'a occurred: the old Muhajir, whose family remained in Makkah and had no protector there, wrote a letter warning the Quraysh of the coming army, and gave it to a woman to carry. The Prophet (ﷺ), informed by revelation, sent 'Ali and az-Zubair to intercept it. When Hatib admitted the deed and swore he had done it only for his helpless household, never in betrayal of Islam, 'Umar sprang up — "Let me strike the neck of this hypocrite!" — but the Prophet (ﷺ) asked: "What do you know, 'Umar? Perhaps Allah looked upon the people of Badr and said: Do what you will, I have forgiven you." And Allah sent down the opening of Surah Al-Mumtahanah, commanding the believers to examine those who come to them for refuge and not to take the enemies of Allah as allies, yet showing mercy to the seeker of security. Hatib was forgiven, and the letter burned.

On the tenth of Ramadan, in the eighth year of the Hijrah, the army of ten thousand moved south. It was the largest force ever led out of Madinah — yet as the Quraysh would learn, it was not an army of vengeance. At Marr az-Zahran the Prophet (ﷺ) ordered ten thousand fires lit, and the Makkan scouts who crept close carried back to the city the terrifying arithmetic of the fires. Al-'Abbas bin 'Abdul-Muttalib met the army on the road, and at his intercession the Prophet (ﷺ) granted safety to those who stayed in their houses, those who entered the Sacred Mosque, and those who entered the house of Abu Sufyan — mercy reaching even the man who had led every war against him.

Al-'Abbas carried Abu Sufyan out to watch the columns pass by night, so that he might see with his own eyes what was coming and carry the news of safety to Makkah. One battalion after another of armoured men in perfect order passed before the astonished Qurayshi, and at last the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) himself in the midst of a sea of Muhajirun and Ansar, their eyes cast down in humility. "O Abu al-Husayn," al-'Abbas said, "this is the Messenger of Allah with his people. Enter the city and testify that there is no god but Allah, for by Allah, if the army takes Makkah by force, your head will be struck." And so the lifelong enemy of Islam entered Islam's camp, and in his house the word went out: he who enters the house of Abu Sufyan is safe.

The Prophet (ﷺ) entered Makkah with his head bowed so low upon his she-camel in thankfulness to Allah that his beard nearly touched the saddle, reciting Surah Al-Fath: "Indeed, We have given you a clear victory." [48:1] There was no battle. The three columns — Az-Zubair from the upper road, Khalid from the lower, Sa'd through the valley — entered almost without resistance; only Khalid's column met armed men from the band of Safwan bin Umayyah, and a brief skirmish at al-Khandamah cost the Quraysh the only lives lost in the conquest of their city.

The Prophet (ﷺ) rode to the Ka'bah, circled it seven times upon his camel, and then, taking the staff of his bow, shattered the idols within and around it — three hundred and sixty of them, toppling one by one — while he recited: "Truth has come and falsehood has departed. Indeed falsehood is bound to depart." [17:81] Then Bilal bin Rabah (may Allah be pleased with him), the former slave who had been dragged across the stones of this city for saying "One God," climbed to the roof of the Ka'bah and gave the call to prayer, and the cry of "Allahu Akbar" rolled over Makkah from the summit of the ancient House. The keys of the Ka'bah the Prophet (ﷺ) returned to 'Uthman bin Talhah, whose family had held the door-keeping from before Islam, saying: "Take them, O Bani Talhah, eternally; no one shall take them from you but a wrongdoer."

Then came the moment the Makkans had every reason to fear. Assembled in the courtyard of the Ka'bah, the Quraysh — Safwan, 'Ikrimah bin Abi Jahl, Habbar, and the very men who had tortured, exiled and warred upon him — stood before the Prophet (ﷺ). "O assembly of Quraysh," he said, "what do you think I am about to do with you?" "Good," they answered; "you are a noble brother, son of a noble brother." He spoke to them the words Yusuf (peace be upon him) had spoken to the brothers who had thrown him into the well: "No blame upon you this day. Go your way, for you are freed." [12:92] With those words, the whole of Makkan society passed from the jurisdiction of vengeance into that of mercy. Of all who had wronged him, only a handful whose crimes were beyond the ordinary — men who had shed blood in cold blood or tortured the believers past bearing, and who refused the amnesty — were excluded; and even most of these were later forgiven when they accepted the faith. Hind, who had mutilated the body of Hamzah at Uhud, was veiled and forgiven; 'Ikrimah, son of the man who had hunted him for twenty years, fled to the sea and was brought back by his wife to the Prophet's protection, and died one of the great Muslims of his age; Safwan, who had armed Banu Bakr, was granted the Prophet's own cloak at the hand of 'Umayr bin Wahab and given months of security, and Islam captured him in the end.

The Prophet (ﷺ) remained some nineteen days in his birthplace, and his rule over it was the rule of a servant, not a conqueror. The muezzin of the Ka'bah was a freed slave of Abyssinian blood; the keys remained with the family of Talhah; the water-bearing with the family of 'Abbas; and when the Prophet (ﷺ) sat, he sat on the ground like any man. One of the Quraysh, watching from a rooftop as the Muslims performed the prayer, understood at last what had entered his city: "By Allah," he said, "this is a kingship the like of which is not of this world." The conquest of Makkah was not the capture of a city; it was the reclamation of the first house of monotheism, and the closing scene of the Makkan era of the Sirah.

Lessons and Reflections

• The Prophet's (ﷺ) entry into Makkah — head bowed low on his camel — is Islam's model of power: victory over a city brought humility before Allah, not triumph before men.

• 'Go your way, for you are free': the greatest act of forgiveness in history was spoken by a man with an army at his back. Mercy at the height of power is the only mercy that proves character.

• The conquest shows that grievances are addressed, not ignored: the Prophet (ﷺ) moved against the violators of Khuza'ah, yet granted amnesty before a single sword was needed. Justice and mercy were the two pillars of his campaign.

• Bilal's adhan from the Ka'bah proclaims the social revolution of Islam: the slave of yesterday stood on the House of Allah, and the masters of yesterday stood in ranks behind him.

• The lesson of Hatib is the lesson of intention: even a grave error is weighed by the heart behind it, and the man of Badr was sheltered by a lifetime of sincerity.

chapters.title: The Battle of Hunain and the Siege of Ta'if
chapters.content:
The conquest of Makkah had come "as a swift blow," as the Sirah says, and the tribes of Arabia understood that the balance of the peninsula had changed forever. Most submitted to the new reality. But the confederacy of Hawazin — with their kinsmen of Thaqif, Nasr, Jashm, Sa'd bin Bakr and Bani Hilal — resolved not to bow. They were the proud stock of Qais 'Aylan, the bravest of Arab breeders and fighters, and they gathered under the command of Malik bin 'Awf an-Nasri, a young chief not yet thirty, to strike the Muslims before their new strength could settle.

Their council at Autas has been preserved because of the old general who spoke in it. Duraid bin as-Simmah, white-haired and war-scarred, advised against what Malik had ordered: bringing the women, children and flocks of the whole tribe to the battlefield. "If you are defeated," Duraid warned, "who will return to guard your women?" Malik answered with the logic of his race: he would chain his family's camels behind the line, so that no man of Hawazin would turn his back — "and if we are defeated, our women and children with us, we shall be the most wretched of people." They encamped at Autas with their households, their herds and their resolve.

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) marched out in Shawwal of the eighth year, at the head of twelve thousand men — the largest Muslim army yet assembled: the ten thousand of the conquest, and the two thousand of Makkah who had accepted Islam with their city. Numbers had made some Muslims confident, and even a new Muslim of Makkah, Safwan bin Umayyah, who had been an enemy only weeks before, lent the Prophet's army a hundred coats of mail, remarking that it was a fine loan "against a day of defeat" — words that would be tested sooner than he knew. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), however, sought his confidence from Allah alone, and Allah would first teach the twelve thousand the worth of numbers.

In the darkness before dawn the column descended the defiles of the valley of Hunain, and the ambush that Hawazin had set along the slopes opened with a flight of arrows. The vanguard broke. In the morning chaos the retreating tide of men swept past the Prophet (ﷺ) — camels and riders crowding upon one another — until only a handful remained around him: among them Abu Bakr, 'Umar, 'Ali, al-'Abbas and his cousin Abu Sufyan bin al-Harith, who held the halter of the Prophet's mule. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) turned upon his mount and called into the rout: "O people! Come to me! I am the Messenger of Allah — by Him in Whose hand is my soul, I am Muhammad bin 'Abdullah!" And then, as tradition relates, he cast a handful of dust toward the enemy, saying: "May faces be disgraced!" And the verse of the Qur'an records what followed: "And on the day of Hunain, when your great number delighted you but it availed you nothing, and the earth, despite its breadth, constrained you — then you turned back in retreat. Then Allah sent down His tranquillity upon His Messenger and upon the believers, and sent down forces you did not see." [9:25-26]

Al-'Abbas, whose voice carried like the clang of a bell, called out the oath of the Ansar and the Muhajirun — "O companions of the Tree! O companions of Badr!" — and from every direction the Muslims turned their camels back into the valley. The fighting that followed was among the fiercest the Muslims had ever known, hand to hand on the slopes; Malik bin 'Awf was driven back upon his own chained families, and the line of Hawazin broke for good. Duraid bin as-Simmah, the old general who had fought Bu'ath, was killed by Rabi'ah bin Rafi'. A portion of the enemy fled to Nakhlah and Autas, where a detachment under Abu 'Amir al-Ash'ari engaged them and where Abu 'Amir was martyred; the greater part fled behind the walls of Ta'if, their highland capital.

The victory left the Muslims the greatest booty of the young state: six thousand captives, twenty-four thousand camels, more than forty thousand sheep, and four thousand measures of silver — all gathered at Ji'ranah under the guard of Mas'ud bin 'Amr al-Ghifari. And the Prophet (ﷺ) turned the distribution into one of the great political lessons of the Sirah. The captives and the bulk of the spoils belonged to the Muslims by right of battle; yet the reconciliation of Arabia required the new converts of Makkah and the wavering chiefs — men like Abu Sufyan, Hakim bin Hizam, 'Uyainah bin Hisn and Aqra' bin Habis — to be bound by generosity. To each of them the Prophet (ﷺ) gave a hundred camels, until the tents of the newly-won rang with praise of "the man who gives without fear of poverty."

The Ansar watched their own share diminish, and a murmur passed through their young men: "He gives to Quraysh and leaves us, and our swords still drip with their blood." When word reached him, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) gathered the Ansar, and what he said to them became one of the most tender addresses in the entire Sirah. He drew his cloak about him and asked: "O people of the Ansar, what is this talk I hear of you? Did I not find you astray, and Allah guided you through me? Poor, and Allah enriched you through me? Enemies, and Allah joined your hearts?" "Allah and His Messenger are most kind and generous," they answered. "Why do you not answer me, O people of the Ansar?" "What answer can we give, O Messenger of Allah, but that all kindness belongs to Allah and His Messenger." Then he spoke the words that ended every grievance: "O people of the Ansar, if you will, you may answer my words: the others went away with sheep and camels, and you will go with the Messenger of Allah. By Him in Whose hand is my soul, were it not for the Hijrah, I would have been a man of the Ansar. If all mankind went down one road and the Ansar another, I would take the road of the Ansar." The men wept until their beards were wet, crying: "We are content with the Prophet of Allah as our portion and our lot." And the young men of the Ansar carried back to their tents the greatest share of all: the company of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and the knowledge that he was one of them.

While the spoils were being distributed, the warring Thaqif had shut themselves behind the fortifications of Ta'if, the city that had once stoned the Prophet (ﷺ) in its streets. He followed them with a detachment of the army and laid siege. It was a new kind of war: for the first time the Muslims brought catapults and hurled stones at the walls, and constructed a covered battering-ram of hides — the dabbabah — under which men approached the gate. The Thaqif poured burning iron and flame upon the engine, and those of the defenders who were Muslims inside the city suffered with the rest; seeing this, the Prophet (ﷺ) forbade the use of fire against them and withdrew the ram. The siege lasted some eighteen days, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), watching from the lines, made the supplication that surprised his companions: "O Allah, guide Thaqif and bring them to me." Some of the besieged came near enough to shout insults; his companions asked leave to answer, and he answered for them, in effect, by forbidding the breach of discipline. At last, seeing the walls unconquered and the season against him, and — as the tradition says — reflecting that perhaps Allah would bring from the descendants of this people those who would worship Him, he gave the order to withdraw, and the army returned to Ji'ranah.

His judgment was vindicated within two years. Thaqif came as a delegation in the following seasons, accepted Islam, and their city emptied of its idols of al-Lat — and of the men who had chased him through its streets a decade before, he demanded nothing but that they believe. Of the captives of Hunain there came to him, after the siege, Ash-Shaima bint al-Harith, his foster-sister of the days with Banu Sa'd, who threw herself before him saying she was his sister by the milk of Halimah; he spread his mantle for her, seated her beside him with every honour, and gave her the choice of the best of the spoils. She returned to her people with captives, camels and sheep.

The captives of Hawazin were still the hardest question. Their delegation — men whose women and children were held at Ji'ranah — came to the Prophet (ﷺ) on the day of distribution and spoke the sentence that decided everything: "The captives are our flesh and blood." "I make a choice for you," the Prophet (ﷺ) told his companions; "I would prefer to return the captives rather than the camels and sheep, for I am waiting for your decision — the captives belong to me, and I share them with you." The Muslims answered as one: "We return the captives to you, O Messenger of Allah." Six thousand souls went free, and the Prophet (ﷺ) ransomed every Muslim captive in the camp with the same release, giving cloaks to the delegates to dress the freed people. The companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) chose captive souls over camels, and Allah was pleased with them, and they were pleased.

Lessons and Reflections

• Twelve thousand men could not win a valley; one man standing firm could. The day of Hunain is the Qur'an's own lesson that numbers and strength avail nothing without the help of Allah.

• The Prophet's (ﷺ) stand in the rout is leadership itself: he did not command from safety but called the fleeing from the very point of danger — 'I am the Messenger of Allah' — and Allah sent tranquillity upon the believers.

• The address to the Ansar teaches the cure for envy: when the heart murmurs at another's portion, remember the greater portion — nearness to Allah and His Messenger — for which all wealth may be traded.

• The Prophet's (ﷺ) gifts to the new Muslims show that winning hearts is not flattery but strategy of mercy: he spent the war's spoils to purchase the peace of a peninsula.

• Ta'if is the lesson of patience between the two visits: the city that stoned him in the tenth year of the Call was spared and prayed for in the eighth year of the Hijrah — his supplication 'O Allah, guide Thaqif' was answered, though it took time.

chapters.title: The Expedition of Tabuk
chapters.content:
The defeat at Mu'tah had shown the young state where its frontier lay, and the reports that reached Madinah in the ninth year were grave: Heraclius, the Byzantine emperor, was said to be massing forces in Syria, and the Arab tribes along the road — Lakhm, Judham, Ghassan, 'Amilah — were gathering under the Roman banner. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) resolved to meet the threat in the far north itself, at Tabuk, halfway to Damascus. It was the most difficult expedition ever called: a march of more than seven hundred kilometres through waterless country, at the height of a scorching summer, against the greatest empire of the age — and at a season when fruit had ripened and shade was sweetest, when every man's wealth was at its most tempting and his couch at its most comfortable. Allah would use the ease of that year to weigh every heart, and Surah At-Tawbah, revealed in its wake, declares the trial eternal: "Those who remained behind rejoiced at sitting back behind the Messenger of Allah, and were averse to striving with their wealth and their lives in the cause of Allah." [9:81]

This was the "Army of Hardship," Jaysh al-'Usrah. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) made the call openly and asked his companions for provision, and what followed is the most striking record of sacrifice in the entire Sirah. Abu Bakr as-Siddiq brought all that his house contained. "What have you left for your family?" the Prophet (ﷺ) asked him. "Allah and His Messenger," he answered. 'Umar brought half of everything he owned. 'Uthman bin 'Affan equipped the army with three hundred camels with their burdens, and a thousand dinars of gold poured into the Prophet's lap, who turned the coins and said: "Nothing that 'Uthman does after this day shall harm him" — and prayed, "O Allah, be pleased with 'Uthman, for I am pleased with him." He gave likewise for the well of Ruma, buying its water and making it free for the pilgrims for all time. The women brought their bracelets and rings; the Ansar emptied their storerooms. Yet the Prophet (ﷺ) himself, at the moment of departure, could only describe the force by its need: "This is the army of hardship," he said — and thirty thousand men, the largest force the Muslims had ever raised, answered it.

'Ali bin Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him) was left behind to govern Madinah, and the hypocrites whispered that the Prophet (ﷺ) could no longer bear his company. 'Ali took up his armour and overtook the column, and heard from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) one of the most cited definitions of kinship in Islam: "Are you not content, 'Ali, to be to me as Harun was to Musa — except that there is no prophet after me? It is not fitting that I go while you remain, except that you are my deputy." Muhammad bin Maslamah was set over the city's affairs, and the Prophet (ﷺ) rode out with Abu Bakr at his side.

The hardships of the road were part of the trial. Food gave out, and the believers boiled the leaves of trees; the Prophet's own she-camel fell behind all the others, and men passed her by until the Prophet (ﷺ) himself, riding her, outstripped the whole column after his blessing. Jabir bin 'Abdullah (may Allah be pleased with him), whose camel could barely walk, has left the fullest account of those days: on the way the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), learning that Jabir had a bride newly married further down the road and little food at home, came to his tent and blessed a pot of barley and a scrawny goat until the whole army ate and was filled — and on departing, prayed over Jabir's marriage: "May Allah bless you, and bless what you have been given." When they resumed the march, Jabir's weak camel outran the Prophet's own. In the wastes the Prophet (ﷺ) warned his men against the haunts of those destroyed before: he passed the ruins of a people of old and hurried his companions past it, saying, "Do not enter upon these people who were punished, lest there befall you what befell them" — a lesson of history delivered on the ground itself.

When the army reached Tabuk, the feared Roman host had not come — whether deterred by the reports of the Muslim advance, or withdrawn by the emperor's own counsel, the battlefield was empty. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) stayed some twenty days, and filled them with statecraft rather than battle. To Yuhannah, the Christian governor of Ayla on the Red Sea, he granted a covenant of protection in exchange for tribute, writing the treaty in his own name as "the Messenger of Allah" — one of the earliest written instruments of Muslim diplomacy preserved in full. The ports of Jarba and Adhruh made similar treaties. To Dumat al-Jandal he sent Khalid bin al-Waleed, who brought in Ukaydir ad-Dumari, the Arab prince who hunted the wild ass by night — taken at his game, spared for his treaty, and soon a Muslim. No battle was fought at Tabuk; the strength that marched seven hundred kilometres had done its work by arriving.

The deepest wounds of Tabuk were not in the desert but in Madinah. While the army was gone, a band of hypocrites under 'Abdullah bin Ubayy built a rival mosque near Quba — ostensibly for the sick and the poor, in fact, as revelation disclosed, a base for those who had conspired against the Muslims the year before and had sworn in the dark that "if we return to Madinah, the mightier will drive out the meaner."
