On his return the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) ordered the structure razed and its timber burned, and Surah At-Tawbah named it the "mosque of harm": "And those who built a mosque for harm and disbelief and division among the believers... will never cease to witness their building as doubtful in their hearts, until their hearts are cut." [9:107] The faithful three who had not set out and had not lied — Ka'b bin Malik, Murarah bin ar-Rabi' and Hilal bin Umayyah — were shunned by the whole community for fifty days, until the earth, "despite its breadth, became straitened for them, and their souls were straitened, and they knew there was no refuge from Allah except toward Him." [9:118] Then came the acceptance of their repentance, revealed to the Prophet (ﷺ) as he sat with the people, and Ka'b, whose story he told ever after as the greatest day of his life, spent all his wealth in charity in thanksgiving — saying that nothing in this world had ever been dearer to him than his repentance being accepted.

The army returned in Ramadan of the ninth year, fifty days after its departure. On the way the Prophet (ﷺ) spoke to his companions the prophecy that measured the expedition's true reach: "There will not remain a house, of brick or of hair, but Allah will cause this Word — Islam — to enter it, whether to the honour of the honoured or the humiliation of the humbled, whom Allah humbles through Islam." Tabuk was the last expedition the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) led in person. What it left behind was not a conquered province but a frontier of treaties, a purified community, and the clear knowledge that the road north — to Syria, to the world beyond — was open.

Lessons and Reflections

• Tabuk was called at the easiest time of year precisely because ease is the truest test: when wealth ripens, comfort invites, and excuses multiply, the heart is weighed.

• The giving of Abu Bakr, 'Umar and 'Uthman shows three levels of generosity — all, half, and more than enough — and the Prophet's (ﷺ) words for 'Uthman show that Allah records sacrifice even when others surpass it.

• The blessing of Jabir's pot teaches that Allah multiplies the little of the generous: a scrawny goat fed an army, and the weak camel outstripped the strongest after the Prophet's (ﷺ) prayer.

• The trial of the three sincere men and the fall of the mosque of harm together draw the line between error and treachery: the lazy are corrected with patience and welcome; the seditious are exposed and removed.

• Tabuk won its victory without a battle: strength held in readiness, treaties kept in good faith, and the empire beyond the desert learned that Madinah could no longer be touched through its clients.

chapters.title: The Year of Delegations
chapters.content:
The ninth year after the Hijrah was called by the Arabs themselves 'Am al-Wufud, the Year of Delegations. After the conquest of Makkah, the defeat of Hawazin and the silent awe of Tabuk, the tribes of the peninsula — who had spent two decades weighing the Prophet (ﷺ) by the measure of their own interests — concluded that his religion was not the affair of Makkah and Madinah but of Arabia entire. From every quarter, riders set out for Madinah: the biographers of the campaigns record more than seventy delegations in the ninth and tenth years, and Madinah, for a season, became the parliament of the peninsula.

The delegations came to learn, and the Prophet (ﷺ) received them as a teacher and a governor rather than a conqueror. With each people he made covenant: those who accepted Islam were taught its pillars and its law, and teachers and governors were sent to live among them; those who remained on their faiths entered treaties of protection with tribute (jizyah), taking their place in the ordered society the Prophet (ﷺ) was building. Three features recur in every account of that year: the gentleness of the reception, the precision of the instruction, and the care that no tribe should feel extinguished — Islam came to the Arabs as a covenant among peoples, not as the conquest of one by another.

The delegations arrived successively through the year. 'Udharah sent twelve men in Safar of the ninth year; Tujayb came soon after; then Bahra', then the tribes of Yemen in their turn — al-Azd, Bani Sa'd Hadheem, Bani 'Amir bin Qays, Bani Asad — until the roads of the south emptied toward Madinah. Some of the most memorable encounters are preserved with their very words.

Adi bin Hatim at-Ta'i came as the son of the most famous Arab of his age — Hatim at-Ta'i, whose generosity was a proverb among the tribes — and as a Christian, and a man who had grown up hating the new religion of Madinah. When his tribe's riders were taken in a raid, Adi fled to Roman Syria and his sister was brought to Madinah among the captives. The Prophet (ﷺ) honoured her, gave her a place and provisions, and released her; she returned to her brother and said to him the words that brought him to Madinah: "You have done what you have done, and by Allah, if you do not go to him, the Arabs will drive you from your land." Adi came in his armour, meaning to impress and to be feared. He was received gently, taken to his sister and his nephew, and then to the mosque, where the Prophet (ﷺ) was sitting among the poor — a woman with a mat, a man with a single cloak. "Why do they not take you with honour?" Adi asked. "Woe to you, Adi," the Prophet (ﷺ) answered, "do you not know the story of your father? Did he not give to every needy one and stand by every oppressed?" And then he told Adi three things: that a day was near when a woman would travel from al-Hirah to the Ka'bah fearing none but Allah; that the treasures of Kisra and Qaysar would be spent in the way of Allah; and that people would compete in building, until the justice of this religion was the one thing left that men sought. Adi bin Hatim returned to his people as their Muslim chief, governed them justly, and lived to see the signs fulfilled, telling his companions in old age: "I have seen the first two; I await the third."

From the Christian highlands of Yemen came the delegation of Najran — sixty riders, their scholars in silk and their deacon in wool, who debated with the Prophet (ﷺ) upon the nature of 'Isa (peace be upon him). When the argument could go no further, the Prophet (ﷺ) proposed what the Qur'an itself had commanded for such a standstill: mutual imprecation, the mubahalah — "Come, let us call our sons and your sons, our women and your women, and ourselves and yourselves; then let us pray earnestly and bring the curse of Allah upon the liars." [3:61] He came out the next day with 'Ali, Fatimah, Hasan and Husain — his own household — and the Christians, seeing whom he had brought, declined the ordeal and settled instead upon a treaty of protection with tribute. They returned to Najran in safety, with a covenant of security for their lives, their religion, their lands and their churches — one of the founding documents of the Islamic law of the protected peoples.

The delegation of Banu Tamim arrived in Madinah with the old Arab vice of pride: they called at the Prophet's door with the clamour of a rival court, and when a poet of another tribe was being heard, their spokesmen demanded precedence. Surah Al-Hujurat came down upon that scene: "O you who believe, do not raise your voices above the voice of the Prophet, nor speak aloud to him as you speak aloud to one another, lest your deeds come to nothing while you perceive it not." [49:2] The scene passed into instruction; the chiefs of Tamim — among them Qays bin 'Asim, of whom the Prophet (ﷺ) said that he was a lord of the Arabs even before Islam — accepted the faith, and the tribe became one of the firmest of the peninsula.

Not all who came came honestly. Musaylimah bin Habib of Yamamah sent word that he was the partner of Muhammad (ﷺ) in the Message, asking for a share of the land after him. The Prophet (ﷺ) answered him with the letter the caliph 'Umar would later re-read to the Muslims after Musaylimah fell at Yamamah: "From Muhammad, the Messenger of Allah, to Musaylimah the liar. In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. The earth is Allah's; He causes to inherit it whom He wills of His servants, and the consequence is to the God-fearing." And to Musaylimah's envoy, who asked what his master had said, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Were it not that messengers are not to be killed, I would have struck your neck." The impostors of that era — Musaylimah and, in Yemen, Aswad al-'Ansi — were answered with a sentence each, and the two sentences proved prophetic: Aswad was killed by the faithful of Sana'a on the very night of the Prophet's own death, and Musaylimah by the Muslim army at 'Aqraba within two years.

Among the envoys the Prophet (ﷺ) sent out in those years, one mission stands above the rest for what it teaches. In the tenth year he sent Mu'adh bin Jabal (may Allah be pleased with him) to Yemen as governor and teacher, and gave him the charge that became the charter of Islamic jurisprudence: "By what will you judge?" "By the Book of Allah." "And if you do not find it?" "By the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah." "And if you do not find it there?" "I will strive with my own judgment, and I will not fall short." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) struck his chest and said: "Praise be to Allah who has guided the messenger of the Messenger of Allah to that which pleases the Messenger of Allah." And then he spoke the words of a man whose time was short: "O Mu'adh, you may not see me after this year. You may pass by this mosque of mine and this grave of mine." The Year of Delegations closed with that farewell note; the peninsula had come to Madinah, and now Madinah's word would go out to the peninsula — and beyond.

Lessons and Reflections

• Islam expanded by covenant, teaching and example, not by forced conversion: more than seventy peoples sent delegations, and each went home with teachers, treaties and judges.

• The Prophet's (ﷺ) reception of Adi bin Hatim shows how faith is invited: he answered pride with gentleness, corrected prejudice with the man's own heritage, and let the signs of truth speak over the years.

• The treaty of Najran is a foundational text of religious coexistence under Islam: worship, churches, monks and festivals were guaranteed by covenant — the constitution of the protected peoples begins here.

• Surah Al-Hujurat's rebuke of the Tamim delegation teaches the etiquette of knowledge: Allah's Messenger is not approached as a rival chieftain; humility before revelation protects deeds from becoming nothing.

• Mu'adh's commission — Qur'an, then Sunnah, then disciplined reasoning — is the standing charter of how the Ummah meets every new question: revelation first, comprehension second, invention never.

chapters.title: The Farewell Pilgrimage and the Farewell Sermon
chapters.content:
In the spring of the tenth year after the Hijrah — March of 632 CE — the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) performed the one complete Hajj of his prophethood: Hajjat al-Wada', the Farewell Pilgrimage. He had come to Makkah as a child, as a young man, as a refugee and as a conqueror; he would now come to it as every pilgrim after him would come, in the two white garments of ihram, answering the call of Ibrahim (peace be upon him) — and on the plain of Arafah he would leave to mankind, in a single sermon, the charter by which his Ummah would live after him.

He had announced his intention in Dhul-Qa'dah, and the news ran through the peninsula that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would perform the Hajj. From every corner the believers poured toward Makkah — with their families, their camels and their pilgrim songs — until the classical accounts count them beyond one hundred thousand souls; Ar-Raheeq al-Makhtum numbers them at one hundred and fourteen thousand. The Prophet (ﷺ) observed 'Umrah and Hajj together in the same season, and his wives performed the pilgrimage with him. Abu Bakr he sent ahead in the season with the proclamation of Bara'ah — recited by 'Ali to the gathered pilgrims on the day of sacrifice — that the sacred months and the House of Allah would no longer tolerate the treaties of the idolaters beyond their term; and so the pilgrimage of farewell was also the year in which the Ka'bah was finally and wholly given over to the pure worship of Allah alone.

On the day of 'Arafah — Friday, the ninth of Dhul al-Hijjah — the greatest gathering of Muslims in history to that day stood upon the plain where every pilgrim has stood since, and from his camel in the valley of 'Arafah the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) delivered the sermon that is preserved in Sahih Muslim, Musnad Ahmad and the other collections, and which every school of law has ever after called simply "the Farewell Sermon." He began: "O people, lend me an attentive ear, for I do not know whether I shall ever be among you after this year in this place." And then, in words that moved from the sanctities of faith to the structure of society, he declared:

"Your blood and your property are sacred to one another until you meet your Lord, as the sacredness of this day of yours, in this month of yours, in this city of yours. Have I conveyed? O Allah, be my witness." Every claim of the Age of Ignorance he trampled beneath his feet: "All matters of Jahiliyyah are beneath my feet, and the blood claims of Jahiliyyah are abolished — and the first of our blood claims I abolish is the blood claim of Rabee'ah bin al-Harith." The usury of the Age of Ignorance was abolished, "and the first of our usury I abolish is our usury, the usury of 'Abbas bin 'Abdul-Muttalib — it is all abolished." The general amnesty of the conquest two years before was now made the standing law of the community: no tribe would again claim the right of blood and vengeance.

On the rights of women he was as explicit as revelation itself had made him: "Fear Allah concerning women. Verily you have taken them as a trust from Allah, and their rights upon you are that you provide for them and clothe them in kindness." On the temptations of the age to come he gave a prophecy: "Satan has despaired of being worshipped in this land of yours, but he will be obeyed in smaller matters — and of those you must beware." And then the inheritance: "I leave among you that which, if you hold fast to it, you will never go astray: the Book of Allah." He foretold his own departure — "I am a mortal; the messenger of my Lord may come to me, and I answer" — and he closed with the question and the covenant: "Have I conveyed? ... O Allah, be my witness." And the multitude upon the plain answered, one voice upon another: "Yes, you have conveyed, you have fulfilled the trust, you have done sincerely." It was in this address that he also spoke the words that levelled all pride of race: "O people, your Lord is one, and your father is one: all of you are from Adam, and Adam was from dust. An Arab has no superiority over a non-Arab, nor a non-Arab over an Arab; nor the white over the black, nor the black over the white — except by piety. Have I conveyed?" And the answer thundered back: "Yes!"

On that same day of 'Arafah there descended upon the Prophet (ﷺ) the verse with which the religion was sealed: "This day I have perfected for you your religion, and completed My favour upon you, and have approved for you Islam as your religion." [5:3] When 'Umar wept upon hearing it, he was asked why he wept at a verse of completion. "I weep," he said, "because we were being told that something is being perfected — and nothing is perfected but that its departure is near." The Qur'an itself had announced that the Message was finished; the sermon had announced that the Messenger was going.

The days that followed taught the rites by their performance. At Muzdalifah he prayed and shortened; at Mina he sacrificed, offering one hundred camels, sixty-three with his own blessed hand — the number of his years upon the earth — and giving 'Ali the rest to complete, then shared the meat of his own sacrifice with the poor of Makkah. He shaved his head and gave his hair to the men of his household to divide; he drank of Zamzam; he made the tawaf of the House. In the days of Mina he gave his last public instructions, among them the words 'Umar would recite to the pilgrims after him: "O people, I do not fear for you that you will associate partners with Allah after me — I fear that you will contend with one another for this world, and it will destroy you as it destroyed those before you."

On the return the pilgrims rested with him at the halting places along the road, where he spoke to the companies of believers and took their covenant of brotherhood, and then the sea of pilgrims scattered to their lands, carrying to every tribe of Arabia the sermon they had heard with their own ears and the rites they had watched with their own eyes. The Message had been completed, the trust returned, the witness taken.

He came back to Madinah in the last days of Dhul al-Hijjah, and from that season the signs of his departure multiplied: the seclusion of Ramadan of that year was doubled to twenty days, and the archangel Jibril reviewed the Qur'an with him twice — where before he had reviewed it once each year. The Surah of the Help, An-Nasr, had come down amid the days of the pilgrimage season, and the companions who could read its meaning read in it the announcement of the end: "When the victory of Allah has come, and the conquest, and you see the people entering into the religion of Allah in multitudes — then exalt Him with praise of your Lord and ask forgiveness of Him. Indeed, He is the Accepter of repentance." Within ten weeks of Arafah, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had begun his final illness; the Farewell Pilgrimage was his testament before his Lord, and the plain of 'Arafah has never since emptied of the Ummah standing where he stood.

Lessons and Reflections

• The Farewell Sermon is the shortest complete charter of human dignity ever spoken: life, property and honour are inviolable; lineage and usury are abolished; and no station but piety raises a soul.

• 'Fear Allah concerning women' placed half of society under the direct covenant of Allah in the Prophet's (ﷺ) final public teaching — the measure by which every Muslim society must be judged.

• The verse of 5:3 teaches the completeness of Islam: the religion needs no amendment and no addition, only the holding fast to the Book of Allah and the practice of His Messenger.

• 'Umar's weeping at the verse of perfection is the believer's own lesson: every completion in this world announces a departure — value your years of worship while they last.

• The Prophet (ﷺ) performed the rites of Hajj as a servant and a teacher at once: learn your religion by doing it, and teach it by being seen doing it rightly.
